blocks.text: 1. Voting Regressor

blocks.alt: Regressor 1 and regressor 2 both feed the voting regressor

blocks.text: Voting Classifier, the previous topic, combined several classifiers by counting votes on a discrete class label, either through hard voting on the predicted labels themselves or soft voting on averaged class probabilities. Voting Regressor is its direct, natural counterpart for continuous numeric targets, and it is, in a genuine sense, even simpler than Voting Classifier, since regression has no discrete class labels to vote on at all.

Instead, Voting Regressor takes the numeric predictions produced by several different base regressors and simply averages them together, producing one final combined numeric prediction. This closes out the Ensemble Learning module by completing the regression side of the simplest possible ensemble combination strategy already covered for classification, exactly the same fixed-rule philosophy, expressed here through averaging rather than voting.
2. The Averaging Mechanism

blocks.alt: Model 1's prediction and model 2's prediction average together

blocks.text: Every base regressor in a Voting Regressor ensemble is trained independently on the full training data, exactly as it would be if used entirely on its own, and each one produces its own numeric prediction for any given input. Voting Regressor combines these individual numeric predictions with a simple average, computing the mean of every base regressor's output to produce the final, combined prediction.

This is meaningfully more straightforward than Voting Classifier's hard-versus-soft voting distinction, since that distinction existed specifically to handle the choice between discrete labels and continuous probabilities, a choice that simply does not arise for regression at all. A regressor's output is already a plain, continuous number, so there is only one natural way to combine several such numbers together: averaging them directly.
3. Weighted Averaging

blocks.alt: A stronger model gets a bigger weight

blocks.text: Just as Voting Classifier supported assigning manually chosen weights to give more reliable classifiers a stronger voice in the final vote, Voting Regressor supports the exact same idea for averaging: each base regressor can be assigned its own weight, chosen ahead of time, so a regressor already known or believed to be more generally accurate contributes proportionally more to the final averaged prediction than a less reliable one.

This remains, exactly as it did for Voting Classifier, a fixed combination rule rather than a learned one: the specific weights are set manually in advance, based on prior knowledge or overall validation performance, rather than being learned automatically from patterns in the training data the way a Stacking Regressor's meta-model, covered in the next section, would learn its own combination weights directly.
4. The Same Variance-Reduction Logic

It is worth explicitly tracing this back to the variance-reduction mechanism already covered in depth for Bagging, and specifically for Random Forest Regression's own tree-averaging step. Averaging together several predictions that are only weakly correlated with each other reduces the overall variance of that averaged prediction substantially, since individual errors, as long as they are not all pointing in the exact same direction on the exact same examples, tend to partially cancel out when combined.

Voting Regressor applies this exact statistical logic, just across genuinely different regressor types rather than across many decision trees built from different bootstrap samples, exactly the same broadening from tree-specific mechanics to a general principle already covered for both Bagging and Boosting earlier in this module. Whenever the base regressors involved genuinely make different kinds of errors on different examples, this averaging step reduces the overall prediction variance meaningfully, often producing a final ensemble that outperforms any single base regressor taken alone.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This variance-reduction benefit depends directly on how correlated the base regressors' errors actually are with each other. Averaging several regressors that all make nearly identical mistakes on the same examples provides very little benefit, exactly the same diversity requirement already emphasized for Voting Classifier and Stacking.

blocks.text: 5. The Value of Combining Different Regression Approaches

Voting Regressor tends to work best when combining genuinely different kinds of regression models, echoing exactly the same diversity principle already covered for Voting Classifier and Stacking. Linear Regression captures a straightforward, straight-line relationship between features and target. Random Forest Regression captures non-linear, threshold-based patterns through its ensemble of trees. Support Vector Regression captures a margin-based relationship, potentially non-linear itself through the kernel trick.

Each of these three fundamentally different modeling approaches is likely to capture a somewhat different aspect of whatever the true underlying relationship between features and target actually is, and each is likely to struggle in different ways on different portions of the input space. Averaging their predictions together lets the ensemble draw on the genuine complementary strengths of each individual approach, smoothing over whichever specific weaknesses any single one of them might have on its own.

blocks.text: 6. A Practical Robustness Benefit

blocks.alt: When one model performs poorly, others compensate

blocks.text: A single regressor, evaluated on a particularly difficult or unusual input, can occasionally produce a prediction that is badly off, whether because that specific input sits in a region the model was never well trained on, or because that particular algorithm has some inherent weakness for that kind of input. Averaging across several genuinely different regressors provides a meaningful practical safeguard against exactly this failure mode.

As long as the other regressors in the ensemble do not happen to share that exact same specific weakness or blind spot, their more reasonable predictions for that difficult input pull the final averaged result back toward something more sensible, rather than letting one single model's badly-off prediction stand entirely on its own. This is a genuinely useful, practical robustness benefit, echoing precisely the same underlying logic that made averaging across many trees valuable for Random Forest Regression back in the Regression module.
7. Voting Regressor versus Stacking Regressor

blocks.alt: Voting uses a fixed combination while stacking uses a learned combination

blocks.text: Exactly as Stacking has a classification form covered in its own topic, a Stacking Regressor variant exists as its direct regression counterpart: a trained meta-model learns how to best combine several base regressors' numeric outputs, rather than simply averaging them with a fixed rule the way Voting Regressor does. This mirrors precisely the same tradeoff already covered in depth for Voting Classifier versus Stacking earlier in this module.

Voting Regressor's fixed averaging rule is simpler, faster to implement, and requires no additional cross-validation or holdout splitting beyond fitting the base regressors themselves. A Stacking Regressor's learned meta-model offers a genuinely more flexible combination rule in exchange for that added implementation complexity and computational cost, one capable of learning that, for instance, one particular base regressor should be trusted more heavily for certain regions of the input space and a different regressor trusted more heavily elsewhere, a pattern a fixed averaging rule simply cannot express.

blocks.text: 8. Summarizing the Classification-Regression Parallel

It is worth summarizing directly how the simplest ensemble combination strategy, voting, plays out differently across the two task types covered in this course. For classification, Voting Classifier needed two distinct combination styles, hard voting on discrete predicted labels and soft voting on averaged class probabilities, precisely because classification outputs come in these two genuinely different forms, a label and, optionally, a probability distribution over labels.

For regression, Voting Regressor needs only one combination style, plain averaging, since a regressor's output is already a single continuous number with no discrete-versus-probabilistic distinction to navigate at all. This simplification is a direct, natural consequence of the underlying task itself, not an arbitrary difference between the two techniques, and it is a useful, concrete example of how the same ensemble principle, combine several models' predictions, adapts its specific mechanics to fit the actual shape of whatever is being predicted.
9. When Voting Regressor Is the Right Choice

blocks.alt: Diverse regressors being available makes voting regressor a good fit

blocks.text: Voting Regressor is the natural, sensible choice whenever a handful of genuinely different, individually reasonable regressors already exist for a given regression problem, since averaging them together is nearly free in terms of both implementation effort and computational cost, and it very often reduces prediction variance meaningfully, exactly the benefit already covered in this topic's Variance-Reduction section.

It is the right starting point whenever a fast, simple, easily explainable ensemble baseline is what is genuinely needed for a regression task, before investing the additional implementation time and complexity a Stacking Regressor would require. When the base regressors show clear, consistent, measurable differences in their reliability across different regions of the input space, differences worth capturing more precisely than a fixed averaging or weighting scheme could manage, a Stacking Regressor's learned combination rule is likely to perform meaningfully better, making that added complexity genuinely worth the investment.
10. Worked Example
The example below builds a Voting Regressor combining three different base regressors, comparing its accuracy against each individual base regressor alone.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import VotingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(200, 1))
y = 2 * X.ravel() + 0.5 * X.ravel() ** 2 + rng.normal(0, 3, size=200)  # a mildly non-linear relationship

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

base_models = [
    ('linear', LinearRegression()),
    ('random_forest', RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)),
    ('svr', make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVR(kernel='rbf'))),
]

for name, model in base_models:
    scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring='r2')
    print(f"{name} alone: CV R2 = {scores.mean():.3f}")

voting_regressor = VotingRegressor(estimators=base_models)
voting_scores = cross_val_score(voting_regressor, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring='r2')
print(f"Voting Regressor ensemble: CV R2 = {voting_scores.mean():.3f}")

weighted_voting_regressor = VotingRegressor(estimators=base_models, weights=[1, 2, 1])
weighted_scores = cross_val_score(weighted_voting_regressor, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring='r2')
print(f"Weighted Voting Regressor (Random Forest weighted higher): CV R2 = {weighted_scores.mean():.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: On a mildly non-linear relationship like this one, Linear Regression alone tends to underfit while Random Forest and SVR capture the curvature better, so weighting Random Forest more heavily in the ensemble often improves the combined result, exactly the weighted averaging idea covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Ensemble Learning Module Complete

blocks.alt: The Ensemble Learning module is complete, Model Evaluation comes next

blocks.text: This closes the Ensemble Learning module, six topics stepping back from the specific algorithms already covered in depth elsewhere in this course, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and their descendants, to examine the general principles underneath them: Bagging's parallel variance reduction, Boosting's sequential bias reduction, Stacking and Blending's learned combination rules, and Voting Classifier and Voting Regressor's simplest possible fixed combination strategies.

Every technique in this module answers the same underlying question, how should predictions from multiple models be combined, with a genuinely different answer, ranging from a simple fixed vote or average, through weighted variants, to a fully learned meta-model. Recognizing which of these general strategies any specific algorithm actually implements, something this module made explicit for algorithms already covered earlier in this course, is a durable, transferable skill that extends well beyond any single library or specific technique.
12. Key Takeaways

items: Voting Regressor is Voting Classifier's direct counterpart for continuous targets, simply averaging numeric predictions.
It needs only one combination style, plain averaging, since regression outputs have no discrete-versus-probability distinction to navigate.
Weighted averaging lets a more accurate regressor count for more, but the weights remain fixed in advance, not learned.
It applies the same variance-reduction logic already covered for Bagging and Random Forest Regression's tree averaging.
It works best combining genuinely different regression approaches, whose errors are only weakly correlated with each other.
Averaging provides a practical robustness benefit, smoothing over any single regressor's occasional badly-off prediction.
A Stacking Regressor variant offers a more flexible, learned combination rule at the cost of added implementation complexity.
It makes a genuinely strong, practical baseline ensemble to try before reaching for a Stacking Regressor's added complexity.

This closes the Ensemble Learning module: Bagging, Boosting, Stacking, Blending, Voting Classifier, and Voting Regressor together form a complete toolkit for combining models. Next up: Model Evaluation Regression, examining how to rigorously measure a regression model's performance.
